status: word-specific content authored; final candidate verification required

words.definition: Paired reproductive organs that support sperm development and release hormones, including testosterone.

structure.text: Irregular plural: one testis, two testes. Testicular is the related adjective. These forms identify the organ; they do not distinguish its internal cell types.

words.whatItDoes: Different tissues within them coordinate sperm development and androgen secretion.
words.commonConfusion: Sperm production and hormone secretion occur in different compartments.
words.retrievalPrompt: Could normal testosterone coexist with impaired sperm development? Explain.

words.definition: Coiled tubes inside the testes where sperm cells develop among supporting cells.

structure.text: Tubules names small tubes; seminiferous specifies the sperm-producing tubes of the testis. Read the modifier with the noun, not as a separate organ.

words.whatItDoes: Their epithelium provides the local setting for the developing sperm lineage.
words.commonConfusion: These are production sites, not the main storage duct.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace where cells go after developing in these tubules.

words.definition: Supporting cells within the sperm-producing tubes of a testis; they nourish developing sperm and regulate their local conditions.

structure.text: Sertoli is an eponym, a personal name used in anatomy; cells is the head noun. The name itself does not encode the cells' supporting function.

words.whatItDoes: They support germ cells and respond to FSH within the tubules.
words.commonConfusion: They are not the principal testosterone-producing cells.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict an effect of damaged Sertoli support despite open transport ducts.

words.definition: Cells between the sperm-producing tubes of a testis that release the hormone testosterone into blood; also called Leydig cells.

structure.text: Inter- means between. Interstitial describes location between other structures; cells names the tissue units. In this lesson the location is between seminiferous tubules.

words.whatItDoes: They respond to LH by secreting testosterone into circulation.
words.commonConfusion: Their position between tubules differs from Sertoli cells inside them.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could an LH change affect testosterone without directly acting on sperm?

words.definition: A coiled duct where sperm mature and are stored after leaving the testes.

structure.text: An anatomical noun: singular epididymis, plural epididymides; epididymal is the adjective. Keep it distinct from the testis and vas deferens in the transport sequence.

words.whatItDoes: Its environment supports sperm maturation before subsequent transport.
words.commonConfusion: Maturation here is not the meiotic production of sperm.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can sperm leave the testis without yet having completed maturation?

words.definition: A muscular duct that transports sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory duct; also called the ductus deferens.

structure.text: A two-word anatomical name for a transporting duct. Vas deferens is singular; vasa deferentia is plural. Ductus deferens is an alternative name.

words.whatItDoes: Muscular activity moves sperm along the transport pathway.
words.commonConfusion: Blocking transport does not necessarily stop testicular hormone secretion.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict which function an obstruction here directly disrupts.

words.definition: A short duct that carries sperm and seminal-vesicle fluid into the urethra.

structure.text: Duct names a passage; ejaculatory is the adjective connecting that passage to ejaculation. The modifier describes its role, not sperm production.

words.whatItDoes: It joins the transport of sperm with accessory-gland fluid toward the urethra.
words.commonConfusion: It is not a site where sperm are formed.
words.retrievalPrompt: Place this duct between its upstream and downstream structures.

words.definition: A duct carrying urine and, at different times in typical male anatomy, semen to the exterior.

structure.text: Urethra is a singular anatomical noun; urethral is its adjective. Do not confuse urethra with ureter, a different urinary passage.

words.whatItDoes: It provides an outward passage used by different systems at different times.
words.commonConfusion: Urine and semen are not normally discharged together.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does a shared passage not imply simultaneous discharge?

words.definition: An external organ containing a urethral passage that can deliver semen.

structure.text: Penis is an anatomical noun; penile is the related adjective. This is an organ name, not a compound specifying every tissue or function within it.

words.whatItDoes: Its tissues support delivery of semen through the urethral passage.
words.commonConfusion: It does not produce sperm.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish delivery by this organ from sperm production.

words.definition: Paired glands that add a substantial part of the fluid in semen; they do not produce sperm.

structure.text: Vesicles names small sac-like structures; seminal connects the glands with semen. Seminal does not mean that the glands make sperm.

words.whatItDoes: Their secretions contribute substances and volume to seminal fluid.
words.commonConfusion: They are glands, not containers producing sperm.
words.retrievalPrompt: Could reduced gland secretion change semen while sperm production continues?

words.definition: A male accessory gland that contributes fluid to semen.

structure.text: Gland names the secretory organ type; prostate identifies which gland. Prostatic is the corresponding adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Prostatic secretion contributes to the fluid environment of semen.
words.commonConfusion: Prostatic fluid is not a population of sperm cells.
words.retrievalPrompt: Separate the gland's contribution from the testes' contribution.

words.definition: Small glands below the prostate that release fluid into the urethra; also called bulbourethral glands.

structure.text: Cowper is an eponym rather than a descriptive root. The alternative bulbourethral glands names their anatomical association with the urethra.

words.whatItDoes: Their secretion enters the urethra and contributes to lubrication and local conditions.
words.commonConfusion: The name is not a label for sperm-producing tissue.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does a gland secretion not establish that sperm are present?

words.definition: Fluid containing sperm when present plus secretions from reproductive accessory glands.

structure.text: Semen is a mass noun for the reproductive fluid mixture; seminal is its adjective. Sperm names cells, not a grammatical plural of semen.

words.whatItDoes: It carries the mixture of cells when present and reproductive secretions.
words.commonConfusion: Semen and sperm are not interchangeable terms.
words.retrievalPrompt: Could seminal fluid be present without sperm? Explain the distinction.

words.definition: A sex chromosome that typically carries a testis-development signal in humans; its presence alone does not establish every sex trait.

structure.text: Y is a conventional chromosome label; chromosome is the head noun. The letter is not an abbreviation for all male traits.

words.whatItDoes: Genes it carries can influence a developmental signalling pathway.
words.commonConfusion: A chromosome finding alone does not describe every sex trait.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must downstream signals and tissue responses also be considered?

words.definition: A chemical messenger made mainly by cells between the sperm-producing tubes of the testes; it contributes to reproductive development, function and feedback.

structure.text: This is a hormone name; testosterone is a particular androgen. Do not treat every hormone name ending similarly as having the same receptor or effect.

words.whatItDoes: Responsive tissues use its signal in reproductive function and upstream feedback.
words.commonConfusion: More circulating signal does not guarantee more sperm production.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how an outside androgen signal could suppress upstream stimulation.

words.definition: A cell or tissue with the receptors and internal machinery needed to respond to a particular signal.

structure.text: Target names the receiving cell or tissue; responsive specifies that it can react to the signal, not merely that the signal reaches it.

words.whatItDoes: Receptors and intracellular pathways connect a signal to a cellular response.
words.commonConfusion: Signal delivery alone does not prove that a tissue can respond.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict the result if a hormone reaches cells lacking its receptor.

words.definition: An infection that can be transmitted through sexual contact; pathogens, symptoms, prevention, testing, and treatment differ.

structure.text: Initialism for sexually transmitted infection. Infection is the head noun; sexually transmitted describes a route of transmission.

words.whatItDoes: A transmissible pathogen can establish infection through an appropriate exposure pathway.
words.commonConfusion: Different infections do not share identical symptoms or prevention limits.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is absence of symptoms insufficient to establish absence of infection?

words.definition: The biological capacity or probability of reproduction, influenced by many interacting factors and not established by one classroom measure.

structure.text: Fertile is an adjective; fertility is the corresponding noun for reproductive capacity. It is not the same word as fertilization, a specific cellular process.

words.whatItDoes: It describes reproductive capacity while recognizing multiple interacting pathways.
words.commonConfusion: A normal classroom indicator is not a guarantee of conception.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name two distinct functions needed beyond production of a gamete.

words.definition: Having two chromosome sets, conventionally written 2n.

structure.text: Diplo- means double; ploid refers here to chromosome-set number. Diploid means two sets, not necessarily two chromatids per chromosome.

words.whatItDoes: Two sets allow homologous chromosomes to be distinguished in meiotic reasoning.
words.commonConfusion: Duplicating DNA does not itself change diploid status.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is a primary spermatocyte diploid after DNA replication?

words.definition: Having one chromosome set, conventionally written n.

structure.text: Haploid is the chromosome-set term for one set. Pair it with n; do not use it as a synonym for an unduplicated chromosome.

words.whatItDoes: One chromosome set describes the products after homologous sets separate.
words.commonConfusion: A haploid cell can still contain duplicated chromosomes.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can a secondary spermatocyte be haploid before meiosis II?

words.definition: A precursor cell in the sperm-producing lineage with two chromosome sets; its divisions can maintain precursor cells and produce cells that develop toward sperm.

structure.text: Spermato- identifies the sperm lineage. Spermatogonium is singular; spermatogonia is plural. The full name identifies a precursor stage.

words.whatItDoes: Its lineage divisions can retain precursors while supplying differentiating germ cells.
words.commonConfusion: It is not already a mature haploid sperm.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how renewal and differentiation can both occur in this lineage.

words.definition: A diploid germ cell that has replicated its DNA and enters meiosis I during spermatogenesis.

structure.text: Spermato- identifies the sperm lineage and -cyte a cell. Primary specifies the stage entering meiosis I, not the mature sperm.

words.whatItDoes: It begins meiotic segregation with duplicated homologous chromosomes.
words.commonConfusion: DNA amount and number of chromosome sets describe different quantities.
words.retrievalPrompt: What separates during its first meiotic division?

words.definition: A haploid cell produced by meiosis I that proceeds through meiosis II during spermatogenesis.

structure.text: Spermato- identifies the sperm lineage and -cyte a cell. Secondary places it after meiosis I and before completion of meiosis II.

words.whatItDoes: It carries one homolog from each pair into the second meiotic division.
words.commonConfusion: Its chromosomes can still consist of paired sister chromatids.
words.retrievalPrompt: What separates when this cell completes meiosis II?

words.definition: A haploid cell produced by meiosis II that differentiates into a sperm cell.

structure.text: The sperm-lineage stem links this word with spermatocyte and spermatozoon. The ending distinguishes the post-meiotic differentiating stage, not another cell division.

words.whatItDoes: Differentiation reorganizes its structure without another reduction in chromosome sets.
words.commonConfusion: Differentiation into sperm is not an extra meiotic division.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can shape change while chromosome-set number stays the same?

words.definition: A specialized sperm cell carrying one chromosome set and able, under suitable conditions, to interact with a developing egg cell.

structure.text: Spermatozoon is singular; spermatozoa is plural. Sperm is also used collectively. The full technical noun identifies the specialized sperm cell.

words.whatItDoes: Specialized head and motile structures support transport and interaction with the oocyte.
words.commonConfusion: Being present does not guarantee successful fertilization.
words.retrievalPrompt: Identify two functions required beyond carrying paternal chromosomes.

words.definition: A specialized cap on the sperm head involved in interaction with the oocyte's coverings.

structure.text: Acrosome is the name of the sperm-head cap; acrosomal is its adjective. The related phrase acrosome reaction names a process involving that structure.

words.whatItDoes: Its contents and membrane changes assist interaction with oocyte coverings.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the sperm's nucleus or its energy-producing region.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why would impaired acrosomal function matter after sperm reaches the oocyte?

words.definition: A long cellular extension that produces movement, as in the tail of a sperm cell.

structure.text: Flagellum is singular; flagella is plural; flagellar is the adjective. The name identifies a cellular extension rather than every mechanism that moves it.

words.whatItDoes: Coordinated bending produces propulsive movement.
words.commonConfusion: Movement is not the same process as sperm production.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict which step could fail if sperm are formed but their flagella do not function.

words.definition: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone: a chemical signal from the brain region called the hypothalamus that stimulates release of FSH and LH from the front part of the pituitary gland.

structure.text: Initialism for gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Releasing identifies its upstream signalling role: it stimulates release of pituitary gonadotropins.

words.whatItDoes: It stimulates pituitary gonadotropin signalling within a regulated axis.
words.commonConfusion: It does not directly perform every gonadal response.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace its effect through pituitary and gonadal targets.

words.definition: Follicle-stimulating hormone: a signal from the anterior pituitary that supports growth of the cells around a developing egg and acts through Sertoli cells to support sperm development.

structure.text: Initialism for follicle-stimulating hormone. The name highlights an ovarian action, but the same hormone also acts through testicular support cells.

words.whatItDoes: It acts on gonadal support pathways involved in gamete development.
words.commonConfusion: Its actions are not identical to LH's actions.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast an FSH-responsive testicular cell with an LH-responsive cell.

words.definition: Luteinizing hormone: a signal from the anterior pituitary that stimulates testosterone release in testes and helps trigger egg release and formation of temporary hormone-producing tissue in ovaries.

structure.text: Initialism for luteinizing hormone. Luteinizing links the name to corpus-luteum formation; the name does not list every gonadal action.

words.whatItDoes: It promotes gonadal responses including androgen secretion and ovarian ovulatory changes.
words.commonConfusion: A basal level and a transient surge are different signal patterns.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does an ovarian LH surge convey more than the statement that LH is present?

words.definition: A brain region that integrates information and releases signals to help regulate the pituitary gland.

structure.text: Hypo- means below; thalamus is an anatomical reference. The positional name does not by itself describe its endocrine control functions.

words.whatItDoes: It integrates information and regulates pituitary stimulation through releasing signals.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the source of every hormone in the axis.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace one hypothalamic signal to a pituitary and then a gonadal response.

words.definition: The hormone-producing front part of the pituitary gland below the brain.

structure.text: Anterior means toward the front; pituitary names the gland. The modifier distinguishes this hormone-producing region from the posterior pituitary.

words.whatItDoes: Its endocrine cells release hormones acting on downstream targets.
words.commonConfusion: It differs from the posterior pituitary's role in releasing hypothalamic hormones.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish the source and target of one anterior-pituitary hormone.

words.definition: A structure directly involved in reproduction, such as an ovary or testis.

structure.text: Characteristic is the head noun; sex identifies the context and primary identifies direct reproductive anatomy. Primary is not a measure of importance.

words.whatItDoes: It identifies anatomy directly participating in reproductive processes.
words.commonConfusion: Primary does not mean appearing earlier on every developmental timeline.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain why a testis fits this category.

words.definition: A pubertal trait influenced by hormones that is not itself a gamete-producing or gamete-transporting organ.

structure.text: Characteristic is the head noun; secondary distinguishes associated pubertal traits from structures directly involved in gamete production or transport.

words.whatItDoes: Hormonal effects can change traits without making the trait a gamete-producing organ.
words.commonConfusion: Secondary does not mean biologically unimportant.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast a pubertal body trait with a gamete-producing structure.

words.definition: Control in which a response reduces the original deviation or lowers upstream stimulation.

structure.text: Feedback names a response returned to an earlier process. Negative specifies reduction of the initiating deviation or upstream drive, not harm.

words.whatItDoes: A downstream response reduces an earlier deviation or upstream drive.
words.commonConfusion: Negative does not mean harmful.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace how a rising downstream hormone could reduce upstream stimulation.

words.definition: A gonadal hormone that provides feedback reducing FSH release.

structure.text: The name connects with inhibit, to reduce an activity. Here the named hormone inhibits FSH release; it does not inhibit every reproductive process.

words.whatItDoes: Its feedback helps regulate pituitary FSH output.
words.commonConfusion: It does not replace every other gonadal feedback signal.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict the direction of FSH change when inhibin feedback increases.

words.definition: A factor intentionally kept consistent so it does not confound the tested comparison.

structure.text: Variable names a factor; controlled specifies that it is intentionally held consistent. Compare independent and dependent variables.

words.whatItDoes: Holding it consistent improves interpretation of the tested contrast.
words.commonConfusion: It is not necessarily the independent variable being deliberately changed.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name a controlled condition for comparing two sperm-development models.

words.definition: A reproductive organ that contains developing egg cells and releases reproductive hormones.

structure.text: Ovary is singular; ovaries is plural; ovarian is the adjective. Oocyte names a cell within an ovarian developmental system, not another form of the organ's name.

words.whatItDoes: Follicular and later luteal tissues coordinate oocyte development with endocrine changes.
words.commonConfusion: An ovary is not just a passive store of mature eggs.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how different ovarian tissues contribute before and after ovulation.

words.definition: An ovarian structure containing an oocyte and surrounding support and hormone-producing cells.

structure.text: Follicle is a structural noun; follicular is the adjective. Ovarian follicle specifies the context, because follicle also occurs in other anatomical names.

words.whatItDoes: Surrounding cells support the oocyte and participate in hormone signalling.
words.commonConfusion: Follicle and oocyte name different levels of organization.
words.retrievalPrompt: What remains of the follicular tissue after the oocyte is released?

words.definition: A developing female germ cell; stage names such as primary and secondary oocyte reflect meiotic state.

structure.text: Oo- concerns the egg lineage and -cyte means cell. The prefix does not specify meiotic stage; primary or secondary supplies that distinction.

words.whatItDoes: Its developmental stage links meiotic state with reproductive events.
words.commonConfusion: Oocyte does not always mean a cell that has completed meiosis.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is a stage label necessary when describing an oocyte?

words.definition: Temporary hormone-producing tissue formed from a follicle after ovulation; it releases progesterone and estrogen.

structure.text: A two-word anatomical name traditionally rendered yellow body. Corpus luteum is singular; corpora lutea is plural; luteal is the related adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Its hormones sustain secretory endometrial conditions during the luteal interval.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the released oocyte.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does loss of its hormonal support relate to endometrial change?

words.definition: A uterine tube that receives an ovulated oocyte and is the usual site of fertilization; its lining and muscular wall support transport toward the uterus.

structure.text: Fallopian is an eponymic adjective; tube is the structure noun. Uterine tube is the descriptive alternative used for the same structure.

words.whatItDoes: Cilia and muscular movements help convey reproductive material toward the uterus.
words.commonConfusion: Fertilization and implantation normally occur at different locations.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace the usual sequence from fertilization to uterine implantation.

words.definition: Finger-like extensions near the opening of a uterine tube that help receive an ovulated oocyte.

structure.text: Fimbriae is plural; fimbria is singular. Fimbrial is the adjective describing the fringe-like extensions near a uterine-tube opening.

words.whatItDoes: Their position and movement help receive the ovulated oocyte near the tube opening.
words.commonConfusion: They are not an impermeable sealed connection to the ovary.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does release from the ovary not itself prove successful tubal entry?

words.definition: A muscular reproductive organ containing the endometrium and supporting implantation and prenatal development.

structure.text: Uterus is the organ noun; uterine is its adjective. The adjective can modify lining, wall or cycle, which are different aspects of the organ.

words.whatItDoes: Its lining and muscular wall support distinct phases of reproductive function.
words.commonConfusion: The endometrium is one component, not the entire uterus.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish a lining function from a muscular-wall function.

words.definition: The hormone-responsive inner lining of the uterus where implantation may occur.

structure.text: Endo- means within; the complete anatomical name identifies the uterine lining. Endometrial is its adjective; it does not name the whole uterus.

words.whatItDoes: Hormonal signals alter its growth, secretion and receptivity.
words.commonConfusion: A thick lining alone does not guarantee implantation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does receptivity involve physiological state as well as tissue amount?

words.definition: The lower, narrow region of the uterus that opens into the vagina.

structure.text: Cervix is a neck-region anatomical noun; cervical is its adjective. In this reproductive context it means the uterine cervix, not the cervical spine.

words.whatItDoes: It forms the lower uterine passage and undergoes changes in reproductive processes.
words.commonConfusion: It is not another name for the vagina.
words.retrievalPrompt: Place it anatomically between the uterus and vagina.

words.definition: A muscular canal connecting the cervix with the exterior.

structure.text: Vagina is the anatomical noun; vaginal is its adjective. It names a canal, whereas vulva names external genital structures.

words.whatItDoes: It provides a muscular passage connecting the cervix to the exterior.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the location of ovarian gamete production.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish this passage from the uterus and uterine tube.

words.definition: A developing oocyte that has entered meiosis I and may remain arrested in prophase I for years.

structure.text: Oocyte names an egg-lineage cell; primary specifies the stage that has entered meiosis I. Primary is a developmental qualifier.

words.whatItDoes: Meiotic arrest separates entry into meiosis from later completion of the first division.
words.commonConfusion: It has not already completed both meiotic divisions.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can elapsed age differ greatly from time spent actively dividing?

words.definition: The cell produced after meiosis I in oogenesis; in humans it is typically arrested in metaphase II until fertilization.

structure.text: Oocyte names an egg-lineage cell; secondary specifies the stage after meiosis I. It does not mean meiosis II has already finished.

words.whatItDoes: Its usual arrest links completion of meiosis II with fertilization-related activation.
words.commonConfusion: Ovulation does not ordinarily release a cell that has completed meiosis II.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which event can trigger completion of its arrested division?

words.definition: A small haploid cell produced by unequal cytokinesis during oogenesis that usually does not become an egg.

structure.text: Body names a small cell-like product here; polar distinguishes the unequal meiotic division product. The phrase does not mean a pole of the entire embryo.

words.whatItDoes: Unequal division separates chromosome material while retaining most cytoplasm in the oocyte.
words.commonConfusion: Its small size does not imply absence of a chromosome set.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does unequal cytokinesis differ from unequal chromosome segregation?

words.definition: Release of a secondary oocyte and surrounding cells from a mature ovarian follicle.

structure.text: The process noun is related to ovulate. It names release from a mature ovarian follicle, not the later process of fertilization.

words.whatItDoes: It moves an oocyte out of its follicular setting into the next transport stage.
words.commonConfusion: Ovulation is not fertilization.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name two events still required after ovulation for implantation.

words.definition: Movement of material along a surface by coordinated beating of tiny cell extensions called cilia.

structure.text: Ciliary is the adjective from cilium, plural cilia. Transport names movement; the modifier specifies movement driven by ciliary action.

words.whatItDoes: Coordinated ciliary beating moves material along epithelial surfaces.
words.commonConfusion: It is distinct from contraction of the surrounding muscular wall.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could impaired cilia affect transport without stopping oocyte production?

words.definition: A blockage that reduces movement through a passage; it does not necessarily stop production upstream.

structure.text: Obstruct is a verb meaning block; obstruction is the condition or blockage. The word concerns passage, not necessarily upstream production.

words.whatItDoes: It reduces passage through a defined route.
words.commonConfusion: An upstream production site may remain functional.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain why a blocked duct does not establish failure of hormone secretion.

words.definition: The chance of a specified reproductive outcome under stated conditions; it depends on many factors and is not established by one classroom measurement.

structure.text: Probability is the numerical chance; fertility supplies the reproductive context. State the specific outcome rather than treating fertility as one guaranteed event.

words.whatItDoes: It frames a reproductive outcome as conditional rather than guaranteed.
words.commonConfusion: A probability requires a specified outcome and population or conditions.
words.retrievalPrompt: What must be stated before comparing two fertility probabilities?

words.definition: The sequence of follicular development, ovulation, and luteal activity in the ovaries.

structure.text: Ovarian means relating to the ovary; cycle names the recurring sequence of follicular, ovulatory and luteal events.

words.whatItDoes: It relates follicular, ovulatory and luteal events over time.
words.commonConfusion: It is related to but not identical with the uterine cycle.
words.retrievalPrompt: Connect one ovarian event to a subsequent endometrial effect.

words.definition: The recurring changes in the endometrium, including shedding, rebuilding and secretory preparation.

structure.text: Uterine means relating to the uterus; cycle here names recurring endometrial changes. Its organ modifier differs from ovarian cycle.

words.whatItDoes: Changes in the lining prepare, maintain or shed functional tissue.
words.commonConfusion: Its phases are not simply names for ovarian structures.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should an ovarian event and uterine response be plotted separately?

words.definition: The ovarian-cycle phase during which follicles develop before ovulation.

structure.text: Follicular is the adjective from follicle; phase identifies a time interval. The phrase connects the interval to developing follicles.

words.whatItDoes: Follicular development precedes the ovulatory transition.
words.commonConfusion: Its duration is not universally fixed.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could variable follicular timing change total cycle length?

words.definition: The ovarian-cycle phase after ovulation when the corpus luteum produces progesterone and estrogen.

structure.text: Luteal links the phrase to the corpus luteum; phase identifies the post-ovulatory interval rather than the tissue itself.

words.whatItDoes: Corpus-luteum hormone output characterizes the interval after ovulation.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the interval of early follicle recruitment before ovulation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which tissue explains the progesterone pattern in this phase?

words.definition: A class of steroid hormones involved in reproductive-tissue function, secondary sex characteristics, cycle regulation, and feedback.

structure.text: Estrogen is a hormone-class name; estrogenic is its adjective. The class includes more than one molecule, unlike the name of a single concentration reading.

words.whatItDoes: Receptor-mediated effects connect hormone levels with tissue changes and feedback.
words.commonConfusion: Feedback direction depends on physiological context and exposure pattern.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is estrogen not adequately described as always causing negative feedback?

words.definition: Control in which a response amplifies the initiating change until an endpoint interrupts the loop.

structure.text: Feedback names a response fed back into a process. Positive specifies reinforcement of the initiating change, not whether the result is desirable.

words.whatItDoes: A response reinforces upstream drive until a terminating event or limit intervenes.
words.commonConfusion: Positive does not mean beneficial.
words.retrievalPrompt: Identify the reinforcing steps and endpoint in a labour feedback loop.

words.definition: A brief marked increase in luteinizing hormone associated with final follicular changes and ovulation.

structure.text: LH expands to luteinizing hormone; surge names a marked transient rise. The second word describes the time pattern, not a different hormone.

words.whatItDoes: Its sharp change is associated with the transition toward ovulation.
words.commonConfusion: A sampled peak may not locate the exact time of ovulation.
words.retrievalPrompt: What can a sparse hormone graph establish about the surge's timing?

words.definition: A steroid hormone that supports secretory endometrial conditions, pregnancy-related changes, and reproductive feedback.

structure.text: Progesterone is a specific steroid hormone name; progestogenic describes related activity. Its name does not specify a universal effect in every tissue.

words.whatItDoes: Its signalling supports secretory uterine conditions and reproductive feedback.
words.commonConfusion: It does not act in isolation from other hormones or tissue responsiveness.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict an endometrial consequence when luteal progesterone support falls.

words.definition: Shedding of much of the functional endometrial layer after ovarian-hormone support declines in a non-pregnant cycle.

structure.text: Menstruate is the verb; menstruation is the process noun and menstrual the adjective. These forms refer to endometrial shedding in a cycle.

words.whatItDoes: Withdrawal of ovarian support leads to shedding of much functional lining.
words.commonConfusion: The entire uterine wall is not shed.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain the sequence from declining luteal support to shedding.

words.definition: A labelled reference line on a graph indicating a variable and its measurement scale.

structure.text: Axis is singular; axes is plural. A graph axis is a reference line; a hormonal axis is a linked signalling system, a different contextual use.

words.whatItDoes: It defines how graph position represents a variable and scale.
words.commonConfusion: A curve's height has no quantitative meaning without its axis.
words.retrievalPrompt: What information must you read before comparing two hormone peaks?

words.definition: A concentration expressed against a reference scale rather than necessarily in absolute chemical units.

structure.text: Concentration is the measured quantity; relative specifies comparison to a reference. It does not automatically carry absolute concentration units.

words.whatItDoes: It supports comparison against a stated reference rather than an assumed absolute amount.
words.commonConfusion: Equal plotted values on separate relative scales need not equal chemical concentrations.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might two normalized hormone curves not be directly comparable in absolute units?

words.definition: The highest observed value in a defined region or interval; sparse observations may miss the actual maximum.

structure.text: Peak is both a noun and a verb. A measured peak is a local or interval maximum; peaked describes the observed curve, not an unsampled value.

words.whatItDoes: It identifies the greatest value among observations in a stated interval.
words.commonConfusion: An observed maximum may miss the true maximum between samples.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does sampling interval limit a claim about peak timing?

words.definition: Differences in the timing or length of reproductive cycles; an illustrative 28-day model is not universal.

structure.text: Cycle names the recurring process; variation names differences among its timings or patterns. Neither word establishes a fixed 28-day schedule.

words.whatItDoes: It describes differences that an illustrative regular cycle can conceal.
words.commonConfusion: A 28-day teaching model is not a universal schedule.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which claim should be qualified when applying a fixed-day diagram to individuals?

words.definition: Methods intended to reduce the probability of pregnancy by acting at defined reproductive steps.

structure.text: Contra- means against. In this whole process name the intended outcome is prevention of pregnancy; the word alone does not specify the method.

words.whatItDoes: Different methods act at different steps in reproduction.
words.commonConfusion: Pregnancy prevention and infection-risk reduction are not identical outcomes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must a comparison state which outcome and mechanism it addresses?

words.definition: Reduction of an upstream signal when a downstream response feeds back on its source.

structure.text: Feedback names the regulatory pathway; suppression specifies reduced activity. Read which signal is suppressed rather than assuming all outputs fall.

words.whatItDoes: A downstream signal reduces an earlier source of stimulation.
words.commonConfusion: A suppressed upstream level does not imply that all downstream functions rise.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace how added androgen can suppress gonadotropin stimulation.

words.definition: A favourable outcome for a specified person, group or system, evaluated using stated criteria.

structure.text: Benefit is an evaluative noun. Beneficial is its adjective; both require a stated outcome and an affected person, group or system.

words.whatItDoes: It evaluates a favourable result against explicit goals and affected groups.
words.commonConfusion: A benefit for one criterion does not remove all limitations.
words.retrievalPrompt: State a criterion needed to compare benefits of two reproductive technologies.

words.definition: A boundary on what a method, dataset or model can establish.

structure.text: Limit is the base word; limitation names a boundary on interpretation or use. Limited evidence is not the same as no evidence.

words.whatItDoes: It bounds how far a conclusion or method can be applied.
words.commonConfusion: A limitation is not proof that all evidence is useless.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name a conclusion a small classroom fertility model cannot establish.

words.definition: A sequence in which sperm and oocyte membranes and genetic material combine to begin development of a zygote.

structure.text: Fertilize is the verb; fertilization is the process noun. In this unit it names gamete interaction, not adding fertilizer to soil.

words.whatItDoes: Cellular interactions coordinate gamete entry, activation and parental chromosome participation.
words.commonConfusion: It is a sequence, not a synonym for implantation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Place activation and implantation in their appropriate sequence.

words.definition: Functional changes sperm undergo in the female reproductive tract that help prepare them for fertilization.

structure.text: Capacitate concerns acquiring a capacity; capacitation names the functional preparation of sperm for fertilization. It is distinct from making new sperm.

words.whatItDoes: It changes sperm function in preparation for later fertilization interactions.
words.commonConfusion: Maturation in the epididymis and capacitation are distinct stages.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can mature sperm still require additional functional changes?

words.definition: Release of enzymes and membrane changes that help a sperm cell cross layers surrounding an oocyte.

structure.text: Acrosome identifies the structure; reaction identifies the coordinated cellular changes involving it. The phrase is a process name, not a second organ.

words.whatItDoes: Membrane and enzyme events assist passage through oocyte-associated layers.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the meiotic division of the sperm.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which barrier-related step does this reaction help address?

words.definition: The protective protein-and-sugar layer around a developing egg cell and the early developing cell group before it hatches from this layer.

structure.text: A two-word anatomical name for the transparent surrounding layer. Zona is singular and zonae plural; keep the whole name distinct from the cell membrane.

words.whatItDoes: This extracellular layer surrounds the oocyte and early conceptus before hatching.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the oocyte's plasma membrane.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must hatching precede normal implantation?

words.definition: Finishing a meiotic division; in a typical human secondary oocyte, meiosis II completes after sperm-triggered activation.

structure.text: Meiotic is the adjective from meiosis; completion names finishing a specified division. State meiosis I or meiosis II when using the phrase.

words.whatItDoes: It finishes chromosome segregation associated with a particular meiotic division.
words.commonConfusion: The term needs a specified cell and division.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which meiotic completion is normally linked to activation of a human secondary oocyte?

words.definition: A haploid parental nucleus present during early fertilization before the parental chromosome sets participate in the first mitosis.

structure.text: Pro- marks a preceding stage here; nucleus is the head noun. Pronucleus is singular, pronuclei plural; each refers to a parental nucleus before first mitosis.

words.whatItDoes: It contains a parental haploid set before the first developmental mitosis.
words.commonConfusion: It is not itself a new diploid embryo.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why are the parental nuclei described as haploid at this stage?

words.definition: The diploid cell formed after fertilization and combination of parental chromosome sets.

structure.text: Zygote is the developmental-stage noun; zygotic is its adjective. It does not name all later multicellular stages.

words.whatItDoes: It initiates the developmental lineage with combined parental chromosome sets.
words.commonConfusion: Zygote and blastocyst identify different developmental stages.
words.retrievalPrompt: What changes between the zygote and a multicellular cleavage stage?

words.definition: Changes following fertilization that reduce entry of additional sperm into the oocyte.

structure.text: Poly- means many; sperm specifies the entering cells; block names a prevention process. It limits additional entry, not the number of nearby sperm.

words.whatItDoes: Fertilization-triggered changes reduce additional sperm entry.
words.commonConfusion: It does not mean that only one sperm ever approached the oocyte.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is limiting additional entry important for chromosome-set balance?

words.definition: Rapid early mitotic divisions that increase cell number without a proportional increase in overall conceptus size.

structure.text: Cleave is a verb meaning split; cleavage is the division-process noun. Developmental cleavage partitions cells without proportional overall growth.

words.whatItDoes: It partitions the early conceptus into increasing numbers of smaller cells.
words.commonConfusion: More cells do not require proportional growth in total size at this stage.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict the average cell-size change during early cleavage.

words.definition: A compact ball of cells formed by early divisions after fertilization, before a fluid-filled blastocyst develops.

structure.text: Morula is a whole stage name; morulae is its plural. Morula and blastocyst distinguish organization, not simply different spellings for any embryo.

words.whatItDoes: Its compact cell mass precedes organization of the fluid-filled blastocyst.
words.commonConfusion: A morula is not yet characterized by the same cavity as a blastocyst.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which structural change distinguishes the following stage?

words.definition: An early developmental stage with an outer trophoblast, inner cell mass, and fluid-filled cavity.

structure.text: Blastocyst names the early hollow developmental stage. Cyst denotes a cavity-bearing structure in this name; it does not mean a disease cyst.

words.whatItDoes: Its cell populations support embryonic development and implantation-related functions.
words.commonConfusion: Its outer layer and inner cell mass have different contributions.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast the future roles of its inner and outer cells.

words.definition: The blastocyst cell cluster that contributes to the embryo proper and some extra-embryonic tissues.

structure.text: Mass is the head noun, cell specifies its material and inner specifies its position within the blastocyst.

words.whatItDoes: Its descendants contribute to the embryo proper and selected supporting tissues.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the sole source of every placental tissue.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should it be distinguished from trophoblast?

words.definition: The blastocyst outer cell layer that contributes to implantation and the fetal portion of the placenta.

structure.text: Trophoblast is the outer blastocyst cell-layer name; trophoblastic is its adjective. Its developmental role differs from that of the inner cell mass.

words.whatItDoes: Its interactions support implantation and fetal placental development.
words.commonConfusion: It does not form the entire embryo proper.
words.retrievalPrompt: Connect its location in the blastocyst with one later function.

words.definition: Attachment and embedding of a hatched blastocyst in a receptive uterine endometrium.

structure.text: Implant is the verb; implantation names attachment and embedding. The process noun does not mean the same thing as embryo transfer.

words.whatItDoes: Attachment and embedding connect the developing conceptus with receptive uterine tissue.
words.commonConfusion: Embryo transfer does not guarantee implantation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must both embryonic and endometrial conditions be considered?

words.definition: A uterine lining in a physiological state that can support blastocyst attachment and implantation.

structure.text: Endometrium identifies the tissue; receptive describes a functional state that permits implantation. The modifier is not just a thickness measurement.

words.whatItDoes: Its physiological condition permits the interactions needed for implantation.
words.commonConfusion: Receptivity is not guaranteed merely by embryo presence.
words.retrievalPrompt: What separates placing an embryo in a uterus from successful attachment?

words.definition: An assisted-reproduction process in which oocytes and sperm are combined or injected in a laboratory before an embryo may be transferred.

structure.text: Initialism for in vitro fertilization. In vitro refers to a laboratory setting outside the body; fertilization is the process being assisted.

words.whatItDoes: It moves specified fertilization steps into a laboratory setting before possible transfer.
words.commonConfusion: It does not guarantee implantation or birth.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which steps still depend on uterine and developmental conditions?

words.definition: Placement of an embryo into a uterus during an assisted-reproduction procedure.

structure.text: Embryo identifies what is placed; transfer identifies the placement step. Transfer and implantation name different operations.

words.whatItDoes: It places an embryo where implantation may subsequently occur.
words.commonConfusion: Transfer is not itself implantation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name a biological event that must follow a successful placement.

words.definition: Human chorionic gonadotropin; a trophoblast-derived hormone that helps maintain corpus-luteum function early in pregnancy.

structure.text: Initialism for human chorionic gonadotropin. Human specifies species context; chorionic links the signal to chorion-associated developmental tissue.

words.whatItDoes: It signals continued early corpus-luteum support.
words.commonConfusion: It is not made by the corpus luteum as its principal early source.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace its source, target and indirect uterine effect.

words.definition: Early embryonic cell movements that establish primary germ layers and body organization.

structure.text: Gastrula names a developmental stage; gastrulation names the cell-reorganization process establishing germ layers. It is not adult digestion.

words.whatItDoes: Coordinated cell movements establish germ-layer relationships and organization.
words.commonConfusion: It is not simply an increase in cell number.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does cell position matter as well as cell division?

words.definition: Movement of cells from one location to another during development or other biological processes.

structure.text: Migration names movement from one position to another; cell identifies what moves. Compare cell division and cell differentiation.

words.whatItDoes: Changes in location bring developing cells into new relationships.
words.commonConfusion: Movement and differentiation are not interchangeable processes.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could normal cell division coexist with abnormal tissue placement?

words.definition: The regulated process through which cells develop specialized gene-expression patterns, structures, and functions.

structure.text: Differentiate is the verb; differentiation is the process noun and differentiated the resulting state. It refers to specialization, not simply separation.

words.whatItDoes: Regulated expression and cellular interactions establish specialized functions.
words.commonConfusion: Specialization does not usually require losing all unused genes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how cells sharing a genome can develop different structures.

words.definition: One of the primary embryonic tissue layers—ectoderm, mesoderm, or endoderm—from which tissues develop.

structure.text: Layer identifies an organized embryonic tissue region; germ here means a developmental origin, not a pathogen.

words.whatItDoes: Its name locates a tissue lineage within early embryonic organization.
words.commonConfusion: A mature organ can contain tissues from more than one lineage.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should organ origin be described by tissue component?

words.definition: The primary germ layer that contributes to the epidermis, nervous system, and selected sensory structures.

structure.text: Ecto- means outer and derm concerns a layer or skin. The embryonic layer name is a positional clue, not a claim that all outer adult tissues share one origin.

words.whatItDoes: Its descendants contribute to surface and nervous-system tissues.
words.commonConfusion: Ectoderm does not mean every tissue near the exterior has that origin.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast the epidermis with deeper supporting tissue.

words.definition: The primary germ layer that contributes to muscle, skeleton, connective tissues, blood, kidneys, gonads, and many reproductive structures.

structure.text: Meso- means middle and derm concerns a layer or skin. The name identifies an embryonic germ layer, not just adult skin.

words.whatItDoes: Its descendants contribute to diverse supporting, contractile and transport tissues.
words.commonConfusion: It is not limited to one mature organ system.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can blood and skeletal muscle share an early germ-layer origin?

words.definition: The primary germ layer that contributes to much of the digestive and respiratory epithelial lining and to selected glands.

structure.text: Endo- means inner and derm concerns a layer or skin. The name describes a germ layer; it does not make every inner organ entirely endodermal.

words.whatItDoes: Its descendants contribute to many internal epithelial linings and selected glands.
words.commonConfusion: An endodermal lining does not make the entire organ endodermal.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish digestive epithelium from its surrounding muscle.

words.definition: Specialized cells and supporting tissue that receive, process or transmit information.

structure.text: Tissue is the organizational noun; nervous specifies information-processing and signalling functions, not an emotional state.

words.whatItDoes: Specialized cells and support structures enable information reception and transmission.
words.commonConfusion: Nervous tissue is not synonymous with every cell in a nerve-associated organ.
words.retrievalPrompt: Connect specialized cell function with one information pathway.

words.definition: The outer surface layer of skin, distinct from the deeper supporting tissue.

structure.text: Epi- means upon and derm concerns skin. Epidermis is the outer skin layer; epidermal is the adjective.

words.whatItDoes: It forms the superficial epithelial layer of skin.
words.commonConfusion: It differs from deeper dermal supporting tissues.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does the skin's layered structure matter when discussing developmental origin?

words.definition: The supporting framework of bones and cartilage in the body.

structure.text: Skeleton is a collective structure noun; skeletal is the adjective. Skeletal muscle uses that adjective but is not itself bone.

words.whatItDoes: Its components support shape, protection and movement with other tissues.
words.commonConfusion: Bone and cartilage are not identical tissues.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how skeletal support contributes to movement with muscle.

words.definition: Tissue specialized for contraction and force production.

structure.text: Muscle names contractile tissue or an organ composed largely of it; muscular is the adjective. The noun does not specify skeletal, smooth or cardiac type.

words.whatItDoes: Contraction produces force within coordinated tissue systems.
words.commonConfusion: Producing force does not mean every contraction produces the same movement.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can attachment and surrounding structures affect contraction's result?

words.definition: Organs and tissues involved in forming gametes, transporting them or supporting reproductive processes.

structure.text: Structures is the plural head noun; reproductive names their functional context. The modifier includes more than gamete-producing organs.

words.whatItDoes: Different tissues contribute to gamete formation, movement and reproductive support.
words.commonConfusion: A structure involved in reproduction need not itself make gametes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast a production structure with a transport structure.

words.definition: The layer of cells facing the internal space of the digestive tract.

structure.text: Lining names the surface-facing tissue layer; digestive specifies the tract. It does not refer to every tissue in the tract wall.

words.whatItDoes: Its epithelial surface mediates interactions with material in the digestive lumen.
words.commonConfusion: The lining is not the entire intestinal wall.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should lining and surrounding muscle have separate lineage descriptions?

words.definition: The layer of cells facing the air passages of the respiratory system.

structure.text: Lining names the epithelial surface; respiratory specifies the air-passage context. The modifier differs from respiration as a cellular process.

words.whatItDoes: Its epithelial surface interfaces with air passages and their local environment.
words.commonConfusion: Airway lining and all surrounding lung tissues are not one tissue type.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain why a mature organ can combine several developmental contributions.

words.definition: Hormone-secreting tissue; different endocrine organs can have different embryonic origins.

structure.text: Tissue identifies the material; endocrine specifies hormone secretion to internal signalling pathways. It contrasts with secretion through an exocrine duct.

words.whatItDoes: It releases hormones that affect responsive targets.
words.commonConfusion: Endocrine function does not identify a single universal germ-layer origin.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why cannot hormone secretion alone establish embryonic origin?

words.definition: The position and order of events relative to a clearly stated starting point or interval.

structure.text: Time is the base noun; timing names the placement or order of events. A starting reference must accompany developmental timing.

words.whatItDoes: A stated reference point lets developmental events be ordered consistently.
words.commonConfusion: Fertilization age and clinical gestational dating use different starting conventions.
words.retrievalPrompt: What must be specified before comparing two age-labelled diagrams?

words.definition: A simplified representation used to explain observations or make testable predictions under stated assumptions.

structure.text: Model can be a noun or a verb. A scientific model represents selected relationships; modelling does not mean making an exact duplicate organism.

words.whatItDoes: It isolates selected relationships to support explanation or prediction.
words.commonConfusion: A useful model does not reproduce every biological feature.
words.retrievalPrompt: Identify one assumption needed when applying a developmental diagram.

words.definition: Information recorded using a specified method; an explanation of its cause is an inference.

structure.text: Observe is the verb; observation is the recorded result or act of observing. The word does not itself specify a causal explanation.

words.whatItDoes: It records what a method detected under stated conditions.
words.commonConfusion: The proposed cause of the observation is an inference.
words.retrievalPrompt: Separate a recorded hormone change from a claim about its cause.

words.definition: A reason the available evidence cannot establish that one factor caused another.

structure.text: Causal is the adjective from cause; limit names a boundary on what evidence can establish about cause and effect.

words.whatItDoes: It identifies missing evidence or alternative explanations that restrict causal interpretation.
words.commonConfusion: Association alone does not establish a mechanism.
words.retrievalPrompt: What additional comparison could strengthen a proposed developmental cause?

words.definition: The extra-embryonic membrane that encloses the fluid-filled amniotic cavity.

structure.text: Amnion is a membrane name; amniotic is its adjective, as in amniotic fluid. Membrane and fluid are different nouns.

words.whatItDoes: It encloses the fluid environment surrounding the developing organism.
words.commonConfusion: It is distinct from the outer chorion.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does enclosing fluid differ from forming placental exchange tissue?

words.definition: An outer extra-embryonic membrane that contributes to the fetal portion of the placenta and chorionic villi.

structure.text: Chorion is a membrane name; chorionic is its adjective, as in chorionic villi. The adjective identifies an association, not the whole placenta.

words.whatItDoes: It contributes to outer supporting structures and fetal placental interfaces.
words.commonConfusion: It does not constitute all maternal placental tissue.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish fetal and maternal contributions to the placenta.

words.definition: An extra-embryonic structure that contributes to parts of the umbilical cord and urinary-bladder developmental pathway.

structure.text: Allantois is the developmental structure noun; allantoic is its adjective. Retain the species context when comparing structures with this name.

words.whatItDoes: Its developmental contributions connect with umbilical and urinary pathways.
words.commonConfusion: Its role in humans should not be copied unchanged from an egg diagram.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must species context accompany an extra-embryonic comparison?

words.definition: A temporary exchange, endocrine, immune, and metabolic organ formed from fetal and maternal tissues during pregnancy.

structure.text: Placenta is an organ noun; placental is its adjective. The adjective can qualify exchange or delivery, which are different processes.

words.whatItDoes: Its tissues support exchange and signalling between maternal and fetal systems.
words.commonConfusion: Maternal and fetal blood do not normally mix as one unrestricted pool.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can exchange occur while the circulations remain normally separate?

words.definition: The connection carrying fetal blood vessels between the developing fetus and the placenta.

structure.text: Cord is the structure noun; umbilical connects it with the navel-region attachment. The phrase includes multiple fetal vessels, not one vessel.

words.whatItDoes: Its fetal vessels connect the fetus with placental exchange pathways.
words.commonConfusion: The cord is not the maternal circulation itself.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace blood movement through its arterial and venous vessels.

words.definition: Transfer of substances across the placental interface between normally separate maternal and fetal circulations.

structure.text: Placental identifies the interface; exchange names transfer across it. Exchange does not require the two circulations to become one pool.

words.whatItDoes: Substances move across interfaces according to their transport properties and gradients.
words.commonConfusion: The placenta is not an absolute barrier to every substance.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does transfer depend on the substance rather than just its presence?

words.definition: Net movement of particles down a concentration gradient through random molecular motion.

structure.text: Diffuse is the verb; diffusion is the process noun. Net diffusion describes the overall balance of movements, not the motion of every particle.

words.whatItDoes: Random motion produces net movement down a concentration gradient.
words.commonConfusion: Individual particles do not all move in one direction.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain net transfer across an interface despite movement both ways.

words.definition: A fetal vessel carrying blood from the fetus toward the placenta.

structure.text: Artery names a vessel carrying blood away from the heart; umbilical specifies this fetal pathway. The name does not promise oxygen-rich blood.

words.whatItDoes: It carries fetal blood outward toward the placenta.
words.commonConfusion: Artery names direction from the heart, not high oxygen content.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can an umbilical artery carry less oxygen-enriched blood?

words.definition: A fetal vessel carrying oxygen- and nutrient-enriched blood from the placenta toward the fetus.

structure.text: Vein names a vessel returning blood toward the heart; umbilical specifies the fetal connection with the placenta.

words.whatItDoes: It returns placentally enriched blood toward the fetus.
words.commonConfusion: Vein does not universally mean oxygen-poor blood.
words.retrievalPrompt: Use direction to explain this vessel's name.

words.definition: Developmental formation and organization of organs from interacting tissues.

structure.text: Organo- concerns organs; genesis names formation or development. The compound emphasizes formation and organization, not merely later enlargement.

words.whatItDoes: Interactions among developing tissues establish organ structure and relationships.
words.commonConfusion: Organ formation and later growth are overlapping but distinct emphases.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can disruption at one developmental stage affect a specific organ?

words.definition: A developing organism in an early stage of organ formation; human stage labels must specify the dating convention.

structure.text: Embryo is the stage noun; embryonic is its adjective. State the organism and age convention when using the stage name.

words.whatItDoes: The label identifies an early developmental stage under a stated dating convention.
words.commonConfusion: The label alone does not identify an exact age without convention.
words.retrievalPrompt: What timing reference is needed to compare embryonic diagrams?

words.definition: The developing human from the ninth week after fertilization until birth, when growth and organ maturation predominate.

structure.text: Fetus is the stage noun; fetal is the adjective. In the human sequence it follows the embryonic period; neither word gives an exact date alone.

words.whatItDoes: Growth and maturation predominate during this named human developmental interval.
words.commonConfusion: Development does not stop when the embryonic stage ends.
words.retrievalPrompt: Describe a continuing developmental change after the fetal stage begins.

words.definition: One of three broad time divisions used to describe pregnancy; biological processes overlap these boundaries.

structure.text: Tri- means three. Trimester names one of three broad pregnancy intervals, not a boundary that every biological process obeys.

words.whatItDoes: It groups pregnancy time into broad descriptive intervals.
words.commonConfusion: Biological events need not start or end exactly at trimester boundaries.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should organ formation not be treated as confined by a calendar division?

words.definition: An environmental agent that can disrupt development under particular dose, route, timing, and biological conditions.

structure.text: Teratogen is an agent noun; teratogenic is the adjective for developmental-disruption potential. An agent name does not specify dose, route or timing.

words.whatItDoes: An exposure can interfere with development under particular biological conditions.
words.commonConfusion: An agent's effect is not independent of dose and timing.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can the same exposure at different developmental times have different effects?

words.definition: The amount of an agent delivered or received, with its units and exposure conditions stated.

structure.text: Dose is an amount noun; dosage describes an administration pattern or regimen. Attach units and exposure conditions to a dose.

words.whatItDoes: It quantifies exposure with units and conditions needed for interpretation.
words.commonConfusion: Dose is not interchangeable with a substance's name or concentration alone.
words.retrievalPrompt: What information is missing from the statement that exposure was high?

words.definition: The path by which a substance enters or moves through a system.

structure.text: Route is a pathway noun. Exposure route specifies entry, while transport route specifies movement through a system.

words.whatItDoes: It specifies an entry or movement pathway relevant to exposure.
words.commonConfusion: Different routes can produce different effective exposures.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must entry route accompany a developmental exposure comparison?

words.definition: Another factor related to both the proposed cause and the measured outcome, which can distort the apparent relationship between them.

structure.text: Confound is the verb; confounder names a factor that can mix up interpretation of an exposure-outcome relationship.

words.whatItDoes: It can create or distort an apparent relation between an exposure and outcome.
words.commonConfusion: Not every unmeasured variable is automatically a confounder.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how a second factor related to both variables could mislead a conclusion.

words.definition: The coordinated process of labour and birth.

structure.text: Parturition is the technical process noun for labour and birth. It is a whole event name rather than a list of its component hormones.

words.whatItDoes: Coordinated hormonal, mechanical and tissue changes support labour and birth.
words.commonConfusion: It is not explained by one isolated hormone acting alone.
words.retrievalPrompt: Connect a mechanical signal with a reinforcing hormonal response.

words.definition: Distension of the cervix that can contribute to the positive-feedback signalling of labour.

structure.text: Cervical is the adjective from cervix; stretch names mechanical distension. In this context the adjective refers to the uterine cervix.

words.whatItDoes: Mechanical stimulation contributes to signalling that can reinforce contractions.
words.commonConfusion: Stretch is a signal, not the hormone itself.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace the feedback from increased stretch to stronger contraction.

words.definition: A hormone made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary; it contributes to uterine contraction and milk ejection.

structure.text: Oxytocin is a specific hormone name; oxytocin-mediated identifies an effect involving its signal. The name is not a synonym for prolactin.

words.whatItDoes: Responsive contractile tissues use its signal in uterine activity and milk ejection.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the primary signal for milk synthesis.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish its mammary effect from prolactin's effect.

words.definition: A locally acting lipid signal involved in processes including cervical change and uterine contraction.

structure.text: Prostaglandin is a class name for local lipid signals; prostaglandins is plural. The historical name does not restrict their action to the prostate.

words.whatItDoes: Local signalling can influence cervical tissues and uterine activity.
words.commonConfusion: Its signalling is not identical to a pituitary hormone pathway.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can locally acting signals matter alongside circulating hormones?

words.definition: Opening of the cervix during labour.

structure.text: Cervical identifies the cervix; dilation names widening. Dilate is the verb and dilated the resulting state.

words.whatItDoes: Opening enlarges the passage during labour.
words.commonConfusion: Dilation and uterine contraction describe different changes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how contraction and cervical opening contribute differently to birth.

words.definition: The birth stage in which the fetus passes out of the uterus.

structure.text: Deliver is the verb; delivery names a stage of birth in this context. Fetal or placental specifies what is delivered.

words.whatItDoes: It describes the stage when the fetus exits the uterus.
words.commonConfusion: Fetal delivery is not the end of every stage of labour.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which major tissue delivery follows?

words.definition: Expulsion of the placenta and associated membranes after the fetus is delivered.

structure.text: Placental is the adjective from placenta; delivery names its expulsion. The modifier distinguishes this from delivery of the fetus.

words.whatItDoes: Separation and expulsion remove the placenta after fetal birth.
words.commonConfusion: It is distinct from the fetus passing through the birth canal.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should birth-stage diagrams include a post-fetal stage?

words.definition: Changes that allow a newborn to exchange gases and obtain support outside the placenta.

structure.text: Newborn identifies the life stage; transition names a change between physiological support arrangements.

words.whatItDoes: Physiological changes shift support from placental exchange to neonatal functions.
words.commonConfusion: It is not only a change in location.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name an exchange function that must change after placental separation.

words.definition: An anterior-pituitary hormone that supports milk production in mammary tissue.

structure.text: Lact- concerns milk. Prolactin is a hormone name linked with milk production; that clue does not make it the milk-ejection hormone.

words.whatItDoes: Its signal supports mammary production of milk.
words.commonConfusion: Production is distinct from oxytocin-driven ejection.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might making milk and releasing it respond to different signals?

words.definition: Production of milk by mammary secretory cells, supported by prolactin; it differs from milk ejection.

structure.text: Milk identifies the product; synthesis means making it. Compare milk ejection, which moves an already-produced substance.

words.whatItDoes: Secretory cells produce the components of milk under hormonal support.
words.commonConfusion: Milk moving into ducts is a different process.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which hormone pathway primarily supports production?

words.definition: Movement of milk into mammary ducts when surrounding contractile cells respond to oxytocin; it differs from making milk.

structure.text: Milk identifies what moves; ejection names its movement out of secretory regions toward ducts. It is not synthesis.

words.whatItDoes: Contractile cells move milk toward ducts in response to signalling.
words.commonConfusion: It does not create the milk being moved.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how oxytocin can alter milk movement without being the synthesis signal.

words.definition: Stimulation associated with an infant feeding that can activate prolactin and oxytocin pathways.

structure.text: Suckle is the verb; suckling names the feeding-associated action or stimulation. It can also describe a young animal, so use the sentence context.

words.whatItDoes: Sensory input can stimulate coordinated production and ejection pathways.
words.commonConfusion: One sensory event can activate more than one hormonal response.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace two distinct downstream effects of suckling.

words.definition: A reproductive-health method that physically reduces movement or contact, with effectiveness depending on the specific method and use.

structure.text: Method is the head noun; barrier identifies a physical mechanism that reduces specified movement or contact.

words.whatItDoes: A physical mechanism reduces specified movement or contact.
words.commonConfusion: Different barriers have different outcome and use limitations.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must pregnancy prevention and pathogen-contact reduction be evaluated separately?

words.definition: A conception-control approach that uses hormones to change ovulation, mucus, endometrial, or related reproductive conditions depending on the method.

structure.text: Method is the head noun; hormonal identifies the type of signalling intervention. The adjective alone does not identify a particular hormone or effect.

words.whatItDoes: Signals alter specified reproductive conditions through method-dependent mechanisms.
words.commonConfusion: All hormonal approaches do not act identically.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must a mechanism claim name the particular method or model?

words.definition: A procedure intended as highly effective permanent conception control by interrupting gamete transport or reproductive anatomy.

structure.text: Sterilize is the verb; sterilization is the process noun. Here it refers to intended permanent conception control, not disinfecting laboratory equipment.

words.whatItDoes: Anatomical interruption is intended to prevent specified reproductive transport or function.
words.commonConfusion: It does not necessarily eliminate gonadal hormone production.
words.retrievalPrompt: Predict a transport effect without assuming endocrine shutdown.

words.definition: An attempt to restore a disrupted reproductive pathway; restoring one function does not guarantee conception.

structure.text: In- negates fertile in infertility; reversal names an attempted restoration. The phrase does not guarantee restoration of every reproductive function.

words.whatItDoes: A procedure attempts to restore a previously disrupted pathway.
words.commonConfusion: Restored patency is not a guarantee of conception.
words.retrievalPrompt: What additional biological functions matter after a duct is reopened?

words.definition: Features that can change, be controlled or be measured in an investigation.

structure.text: Variable is singular; variables is plural. Independent, dependent and controlled identify different investigative roles.

words.whatItDoes: They identify what is changed, held constant or measured in an investigation.
words.commonConfusion: Those roles should not be conflated.
words.retrievalPrompt: Assign distinct roles to three features of a controlled reproductive model.

words.definition: Examination of similarities and differences between specified conditions or observations.

structure.text: Compare is the verb; comparison names examination of similarities and differences under stated conditions.

words.whatItDoes: Defined conditions make differences and similarities interpretable.
words.commonConfusion: A comparison without comparable measurements can mislead.
words.retrievalPrompt: What must be held consistent when comparing hormone graphs?

words.definition: Recorded observations or measurements with their context, units and method.

structure.text: Data is conventionally the plural of datum, though often used collectively. A dataset is an organized collection; the word does not itself establish causation.

words.whatItDoes: Context and measurement methods determine how recorded values can be interpreted.
words.commonConfusion: A collection of numbers is not automatically causal evidence.
words.retrievalPrompt: What units and timing information belong with hormone measurements?

words.definition: A reasoned change to a prediction, explanation or plan after considering evidence or feedback.

structure.text: Revise is the verb; revision names a reasoned change to an earlier account. It does not mean erasing the evidence that prompted the change.

words.whatItDoes: It updates an explanation in response to evidence while retaining traceable reasoning.
words.commonConfusion: Revision is not arbitrary replacement without a reason.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which new observation would justify revising your original pathway explanation?

words.definition: A steroid substance with actions related to testosterone; an outside androgen signal can alter feedback and suppress normal sperm production.

structure.text: Steroid names a chemical class; anabolic describes tissue-building-related effects. The modifier does not establish that exposure improves normal reproductive function.

words.whatItDoes: An outside androgen signal can change the feedback controlling endogenous reproductive stimulation.
words.commonConfusion: Increased androgen exposure does not guarantee increased sperm production.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace a feedback explanation for reduced sperm production despite an added androgen signal.

words.definition: A protein hormone released by the anterior pituitary that contributes to growth and metabolism; also called hGH or somatotropin.

structure.text: Hormone is the signalling noun; growth identifies a prominent action. GH is the initialism; hGH adds human, and somatotropin is an alternative name.

words.whatItDoes: Its signalling contributes to coordinated growth and metabolic effects.
words.commonConfusion: It is not a substitute name for a gonadotropin.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish its source from the targets of LH and FSH.

words.definition: A term sometimes used for age-associated testicular hormone changes; it does not mean an abrupt universal cessation of sperm production.

structure.text: Andro- concerns male biology; pause suggests reduced activity. The whole term must not be read as an abrupt universal end to sperm production.

words.whatItDoes: It describes some age-associated hormone changes rather than a universal abrupt reproductive endpoint.
words.commonConfusion: It is not a direct male equivalent of cessation of menstrual cycles.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should this label not imply that sperm production stops at one fixed age?

words.definition: The end of recurring menstrual cycles associated with loss of ovarian follicular function; the preceding transition can involve changing cycles and hormones.

structure.text: Menopause is the name of the end of menstrual cycling; menopausal is its adjective. Distinguish the endpoint from the preceding transition.

words.whatItDoes: Declining follicular function changes ovarian cycling and endocrine feedback.
words.commonConfusion: The preceding transition is not necessarily one abrupt uniform event.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can changing ovarian feedback alter pituitary stimulation?

words.definition: The developmental process in which the neural plate folds and forms the neural tube, a foundation of the central nervous system.

structure.text: Neural relates to nervous tissue; neurulation names early neural-tube formation. The process noun is distinct from gastrulation.

words.whatItDoes: Folding and closure organize tissue that develops into the central nervous system.
words.commonConfusion: It is not identical with gastrulation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Place neural-plate folding after establishment of the relevant germ layer.

words.definition: A thickened region of embryonic ectoderm that folds during early nervous-system development.

structure.text: Plate names a flattened tissue region; neural identifies its developmental nervous-system role.

words.whatItDoes: This organized ectodermal region participates in folding toward a neural tube.
words.commonConfusion: A plate and a tube are different structural stages.
words.retrievalPrompt: Describe the shape change that connects the two terms.

words.definition: An embryonic structure formed through neural-plate folding that gives rise to the brain and spinal cord.

structure.text: Tube names the shape; neural identifies the developing nervous-system tissue. Plate and tube describe different structural stages.

words.whatItDoes: Its developmental regions contribute to the brain and spinal cord.
words.commonConfusion: It does not become every tissue in the body.
words.retrievalPrompt: Connect its embryonic origin with the central nervous system.

words.definition: Placement of sperm in the reproductive tract to assist fertilization within the body.

structure.text: Insemination names placement of sperm; artificial specifies assistance rather than intercourse. The phrase does not imply that fertilization itself occurs outside the body.

words.whatItDoes: Placement assists sperm access while fertilization can still occur within the body.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the same procedure as laboratory fertilization.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast where fertilization occurs in this approach and IVF.
